query: Federal Reserve interest rate impact on data-center REITs sector performance 2025 2026 earnings call transcript
normalized: 2025 2026 call center data earnings federal impact interest performance rate reits reserve sector transcript

output.content:
**Bottom line:** Federal Reserve policy was an important valuation and financing variable for data-center REITs in 2025–26, but it did not determine sector returns by itself: exceptional AI/cloud leasing demand and backlog conversion increasingly outweighed rate sensitivity in 2026. [[1]]

**Rate backdrop.** The fed-funds target range began 2025 at 4.25%–4.50%, was lowered to 3.50%–3.75% at the December 9–10, 2025 FOMC meeting, and stood at 3.75%–4.00% after the Fed’s September 2026 increase. [[2]] [[3]] [[4]] This path reduced the short-rate burden versus early 2025, but 2026’s renewed tightening—and persistently elevated long-term funding costs—limited the simple “rate cuts equal REIT upside” narrative. [[5]] [[4]]

**Sector performance versus operating performance.** Data-center REIT total performance was weak in 2025, at **-14.2%**, even though the sector generated **21.3% year-over-year FFO growth** and **7.2% NOI growth** in 1Q25. [[1]] [[6]] That divergence indicates that investors discounted the sector for capital-intensity, required returns, and financing/valuation risk rather than a deterioration in underlying occupancy or demand. [[1]] [[6]] By mid-2026, data centers had become one of the best-performing REIT property types, with a **33.2%** return, while 1Q26 sector FFO and NOI grew **29.4%** and **15.8%**, respectively. [[1]] In other words, the 2026 rerating was supported principally by accelerating cash-flow fundamentals and AI demand, with the less restrictive 2025 rate level acting as a helpful, but not sufficient, tailwind. [[1]]

**How rates transmit to the sector.** Higher risk-free rates can lower REIT equity values through higher discount rates and can compress development spreads by raising the cost of debt and equity needed to build power-intensive capacity. [[7]] [[8]] The effect is especially relevant for data-center REITs because the current investment cycle requires very large up-front development expenditures before facilities stabilize and cash rent commences. [[9]] [[7]] Conversely, lower borrowing rates would improve incremental project economics, refinancing costs, and relative dividend attractiveness, although companies with fixed-rate debt do not receive the full benefit immediately. [[10]]

**Digital Realty: earnings-call and balance-sheet evidence.** Digital Realty reported **$18.4 billion** of total debt at December 31, 2025, net debt/adjusted EBITDA of **4.9x**, and fixed-charge coverage of **4.5x**; it expected 2026 long-term debt issuance of **$1.0–$1.5 billion** at **4.0%–4.5%** pricing. [[10]] These figures show why rate levels matter materially to Digital Realty’s marginal funding cost, even though its leverage and coverage metrics gave it capacity to continue investing. [[10]] Management’s Q3 2025 call also explicitly identified **lower interest income associated with lower rates and cash balances** as a fourth-quarter Core FFO headwind—an important offset to the usual lower-rate benefit for a REIT. [[11]] 

Digital Realty nevertheless delivered strong operating results: 4Q25 Core FFO was **$1.86 per share** versus **$1.73** a year earlier, and its initial 2026 Core FFO outlook was **$7.90–$8.00 per share**. [[12]] [[10]] By Q2 2026 it had raised Core FFO guidance excluding promote income to **$8.15–$8.20 per share**, while total debt was about **$18.6 billion**, net debt/adjusted EBITDA was **4.7x**, and fixed-charge coverage was **5.2x**. [[13]] The practical conclusion is that robust commencements, leasing spreads, and fee income more than offset the rate-related headwinds during this period. [[11]] [[13]]

**Equinix: capital-cost pressure is more forward-looking.** Equinix’s Q1 2026 call emphasized that management expected to prioritize debt over equity for capital reinvestment, using its BBB+ rating and balance-sheet flexibility. [[14]] In the Q2 2026 call, management said it expected financing to come from retained cash flow plus debt, projected leverage to rise by roughly **one turn** through the planning period, and estimated that its blended cost of capital would rise by roughly **150 basis points**. [[9]] This is the clearest transcript evidence that even a strong data-center operator cannot fully escape the financing impact of high rates and a debt-funded AI-capex cycle. [[9]] Equinix’s total debt reached **$23.356 billion** at June 2026, while quarterly interest expense was **$151 million**, up from **$148 million** in Q1. [[7]] [[8]] 

Yet operating momentum remained strong: Equinix reported Q2 2026 revenue of **$2.6 billion**, recurring revenue of **$2.4 billion**, and raised 2026 AFFO-per-share growth guidance to **12%–13%** year over year. [[9]] [[15]] The earnings-call implication is that management views incremental investment returns and contracted demand as sufficiently attractive to absorb a higher cost of capital. [[9]]

**Investment interpretation.** For 2025, the evidence supports viewing rates as a dominant valuation and capital-allocation overhang that outweighed very good reported fundamentals. [[1]] [[6]] For 2026, rate sensitivity remained real—particularly for debt-financed development and future refinancing—but record leasing, price increases, backlog conversion, and AI-related demand became the larger drivers of earnings and share-price performance. [[1]] [[9]] The key risk going forward is not merely the Fed’s policy rate; it is whether long-term borrowing costs and required returns stay above the yields generated on massive new data-center builds. [[9]] [[10]]
